subtopic: Definite integral as the limit of a sum, the general form
concept_tested: Reading the general limit of a sum definition of a definite integral
stem: Let $f$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ and let $h = \dfrac{b - a}{n}$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ is defined as

distractor_rationale.A: The student drops the width $h$ of each strip and adds only the heights.
distractor_rationale.B: The student sends $h$ to infinity instead of $n$, reversing the role of the two symbols.
distractor_rationale.D: The student measures the sample points from the upper limit instead of the lower limit.

solution: Divide $[a, b]$ into $n$ subintervals of equal width $h = \dfrac{b - a}{n}$. The $r$th subinterval is $\left[a + (r-1)h,\ a + rh\right]$, and taking its right endpoint $a + rh$ as the sample point, the rectangle on it has area $h\,f(a + rh)$. The total area of the $n$ rectangles is $h\sum_{r=1}^{n} f(a + rh)$. As $n \to \infty$ the width $h \to 0$ and this sum tends to the definite integral. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} h\left[f(a + h) + f(a + 2h) + \cdots + f(a + nh)\right]$. Note that the limit is taken as $n \to \infty$, not as $h \to \infty$, and that the factor $h$ in front is essential because each term is an area, not a height.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} h\sum_{r=1}^{n} f(a + rh)$, where $h = \dfrac{b - a}{n}$.
common_misconception: The student omits the strip width $h$ and treats the definite integral as a limit of a sum of function values alone.

subtopic: Definite integral as the limit of a sum, the general form
concept_tested: Identifying the strip width h for given limits of integration
stem: When $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{4} f(x)\,dx$ is written as $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} h\sum_{r=1}^{n} f(1 + rh)$, the value of $h$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student takes only the upper limit and ignores the lower limit.
distractor_rationale.B: The student adds the two limits instead of subtracting them.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses the lower limit as the length of the interval.

solution: Here $a = 1$ and $b = 4$, so the interval $[1, 4]$ has length $b - a = 4 - 1 = 3$. Dividing it into $n$ equal parts gives each part the width $h = \dfrac{3}{n}$. This is consistent with the sample points $1 + rh$ used in the sum, since for $r = n$ the point is $1 + n \cdot \dfrac{3}{n} = 4$, which is exactly the upper limit. Had $h$ been $\dfrac{4}{n}$, the last sample point would have been $5$, outside the interval of integration.
formula_principle: In the limit of a sum form of $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$, the width of each of the $n$ equal subintervals is $h = \dfrac{b - a}{n}$.
common_misconception: The student reads $h$ off the upper limit alone instead of computing $\dfrac{b - a}{n}$.

subtopic: Definite integral as the limit of a sum, the general form
concept_tested: Recognising a given limit of a sum as a definite integral over [0, 1]
stem: The limit $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{r=1}^{n} \dfrac{n}{n^{2} + r^{2}}$ can be written as

distractor_rationale.B: The student cancels one power of $n$ carelessly and loses the square in the denominator.
distractor_rationale.C: The student keeps $n$ as the upper limit instead of letting $\dfrac{r}{n}$ become the variable on $[0, 1]$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student divides only the denominator by $n^{2}$ and leaves an extra factor in the numerator.

solution: Divide the numerator and the denominator of each term by $n^{2}$: $\dfrac{n}{n^{2} + r^{2}} = \dfrac{1/n}{1 + \left(r/n\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{n} \cdot \dfrac{1}{1 + \left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)^{2}}$. So the sum is $\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n} f\!\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)$ with $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}$. Comparing with the definition on $[0, 1]$, where $h = \dfrac{1}{n}$ and the sample points are $0 + rh = \dfrac{r}{n}$, the limit is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx$. Its value is $\left[\tan^{-1}x\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
formula_principle: If a sum can be arranged as $\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n} f\!\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)$, then its limit as $n \to \infty$ is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\,dx$.
common_misconception: The student fails to factor out $\dfrac{1}{n}$ before replacing $\dfrac{r}{n}$ by $x$, so the integrand and the limits come out wrong.

subtopic: Evaluating a simple definite integral as a limit of a sum
concept_tested: Using the sum of squares formula to evaluate a definite integral from first principles
stem: By the method of limit of a sum, $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} x^{2}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.B: The student uses $\sum r$ in place of $\sum r^{2}$, so the integrand is effectively taken as $x$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student replaces $2n + 1$ by $n$ in the sum of squares formula and loses a factor of $2$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student uses $\dfrac{2n^{3}}{3}$ for the sum of squares, doubling the leading coefficient.

solution: Here $a = 0$, $b = 1$, so $h = \dfrac{1}{n}$ and the sample points are $rh = \dfrac{r}{n}$. Then $h\sum_{r=1}^{n} f(rh) = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n} \dfrac{r^{2}}{n^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{n^{3}}\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^{2} = \dfrac{1}{n^{3}} \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$. Simplifying, this is $\dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{6}\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{n}\right)\left(2 + \dfrac{1}{n}\right)$. Letting $n \to \infty$, the value is $\dfrac{1}{6}(1)(2) = \dfrac{1}{3}$. This agrees with $\left[\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} h\sum_{r=1}^{n} f(a + rh)$ with $h = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$, together with $\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^{2} = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$.
common_misconception: The student quotes the sum of the first $n$ natural numbers instead of the sum of their squares.

subtopic: Evaluating a simple definite integral as a limit of a sum
concept_tested: Handling a non-zero lower limit in the limit of a sum method
stem: By the method of limit of a sum, $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3} x\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student takes the sample points as $rh$ instead of $1 + rh$, dropping the lower limit.
distractor_rationale.B: The student uses $h = \dfrac{b+a}{n}$, so the strip width is doubled.
distractor_rationale.C: The student evaluates $\dfrac{b^{2}}{2}$ only and never subtracts the contribution of the lower limit.

solution: Here $a = 1$, $b = 3$ and $f(x) = x$, so $h = \dfrac{2}{n}$ and the sample points are $1 + rh$. Then $h\sum_{r=1}^{n} (1 + rh) = h\left[n + h\sum_{r=1}^{n} r\right] = h\,n + h^{2}\,\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Substituting $h = \dfrac{2}{n}$ gives $2 + \dfrac{4}{n^{2}} \cdot \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} = 2 + \dfrac{2(n+1)}{n} = 2 + 2\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{n}\right)$. Letting $n \to \infty$, the value is $2 + 2 = 4$. This agrees with $\left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{3} = \dfrac{9}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} = 4$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} h\sum_{r=1}^{n} f(a + rh)$ with $h = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$, together with $\sum_{r=1}^{n} r = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.
common_misconception: The student forgets that the sample points start from the lower limit $a$ and writes $f(rh)$ instead of $f(a + rh)$.

subtopic: Evaluating a simple definite integral as a limit of a sum
concept_tested: Converting a sum with a shifted denominator into a definite integral and evaluating it
stem: The value of $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} \left[\dfrac{1}{n+1} + \dfrac{1}{n+2} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{2n}\right]$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student writes the last term as $\dfrac{1}{n + n/2}$ and gets the upper limit $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student replaces every term by its largest value $\dfrac{1}{n}$ and multiplies by $\dfrac{n}{2}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student takes the sample points as $\dfrac{2r}{n}$ and stretches the interval to $[0, 2]$.

solution: The general term is $\dfrac{1}{n + r}$ for $r = 1, 2, \ldots, n$, since $r = n$ gives $\dfrac{1}{2n}$, the last term. Take out $\dfrac{1}{n}$: $\dfrac{1}{n + r} = \dfrac{1}{n}\cdot \dfrac{1}{1 + \dfrac{r}{n}}$. Hence the sum is $\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n} f\!\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)$ with $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+x}$, and its limit is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1+x}\,dx = \left[\log|1+x|\right]_{0}^{1} = \log 2 - \log 1 = \log 2$.
formula_principle: A sum of the form $\dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n} f\!\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)$ tends to $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} f(x)\,dx$ as $n \to \infty$.
common_misconception: The student does not extract the factor $\dfrac{1}{n}$ from the general term, so the sum is never put into the standard limit of a sum form.

subtopic: The fundamental theorem of integral calculus
concept_tested: Stating the fundamental theorem of integral calculus correctly
stem: Let $f$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ and let $F$ be such that $F'(x) = f(x)$ on $[a, b]$. The fundamental theorem of integral calculus states that $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.B: The student subtracts in the wrong order, evaluating at the lower limit first.
distractor_rationale.C: The student adds the two boundary values instead of subtracting them.
distractor_rationale.D: The student differentiates the antiderivative once more before substituting the limits.

solution: The theorem links the definite integral, which is defined as a limit of a sum, with the antiderivative. Once any antiderivative $F$ of $f$ is known, the definite integral is found by substituting the upper limit and then subtracting the value at the lower limit, in that order. The notation $\left[F(x)\right]_{a}^{b}$ is shorthand for exactly this. Reversing the order changes the sign of the answer, which is why $\displaystyle\int_{b}^{a} f(x)\,dx = -\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$. Substituting into $F'$ rather than $F$ would return values of $f$, not the integral.
formula_principle: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $F$ is any antiderivative of $f$ on $[a, b]$, then $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \left[F(x)\right]_{a}^{b} = F(b) - F(a)$.
common_misconception: The student substitutes the lower limit first, obtaining an answer with the wrong sign.

subtopic: The fundamental theorem of integral calculus
concept_tested: Applying the theorem when only two values of the antiderivative are given
stem: A function $F$ satisfies $F'(x) = f(x)$ for every $x$ in $[2, 5]$, with $F(2) = 7$ and $F(5) = 3$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student computes $F(2) - F(5)$, substituting the lower limit first.
distractor_rationale.B: The student adds the two given values of $F$ instead of subtracting them.
distractor_rationale.D: The student adds the values and then attaches the sign of the difference.

solution: Since $F' = f$ on $[2, 5]$, the function $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ there, so the fundamental theorem applies directly: $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx = F(5) - F(2) = 3 - 7 = -4$. No formula for $f$ is needed. A negative value is perfectly acceptable, since a definite integral is a signed quantity and here $F$ decreases over the interval, which means $f$ is negative on average.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$, where $F$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on $[a, b]$.
common_misconception: The student subtracts the value at the upper limit from the value at the lower limit, reversing the sign.

subtopic: The fundamental theorem of integral calculus
concept_tested: Recognising that the theorem needs the integrand to be continuous on the whole interval
stem: A student writes $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^{1} = -1 - 1 = -2$. The correct comment on this working is

options.A: The working is correct, because $-\dfrac{1}{x}$ is an antiderivative of $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$.
options.B: The answer should be $2$, because the sign is lost while substituting the lower limit.
options.C: The answer should be $\log|x|$ evaluated between the two limits, because $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$ integrates to a logarithm.
options.D: The fundamental theorem does not apply, because the integrand is not continuous at $x = 0$, which lies in $[-1, 1]$.

correct_answer_text: The fundamental theorem does not apply, because the integrand is not continuous at $x = 0$, which lies in $[-1, 1]$.

distractor_rationale.A: The student checks only that the antiderivative is right and never tests the hypothesis of the theorem.
distractor_rationale.B: The student assumes the only defect is an arithmetic slip in the substitution.
distractor_rationale.C: The student confuses the integral of $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$ with that of $\dfrac{1}{x}$.

solution: The antiderivative is indeed correct: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right] = \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$ wherever $x \ne 0$. The defect is in the hypothesis. The integrand $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$ is not defined at $x = 0$, and $0$ lies between the limits $-1$ and $1$, so the integrand is not continuous on $[-1, 1]$ and the fundamental theorem cannot be applied. The absurdity of the printed answer confirms this: $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}} > 0$ everywhere it is defined, so any sensible value of the integral would have to be positive, yet the working produces $-2$. The correct response is to reject the working, not to repair its arithmetic.
formula_principle: The fundamental theorem of integral calculus requires $f$ to be continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$. If the integrand is undefined at an interior point, the theorem cannot be used.
common_misconception: The student applies the fundamental theorem without checking that the integrand is continuous throughout the interval of integration.

subtopic: The fundamental theorem of integral calculus
concept_tested: Finding an unknown limit of integration from a given value of the integral
stem: If $k > 1$ and $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{k} \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = \log 3$, then $k$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student writes $\log k = 3$ instead of $\log k = \log 3$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student equates $k$ itself with the value of the integral.
distractor_rationale.C: The student integrates $\dfrac{1}{x}$ as $\log\left|\dfrac{1}{x}\right|$ and inverts the answer.

solution: For $x$ in $[1, k]$ with $k > 1$ the integrand is continuous and positive, so the fundamental theorem applies: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{k} \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = \left[\log|x|\right]_{1}^{k} = \log k - \log 1 = \log k$. Setting this equal to $\log 3$ gives $\log k = \log 3$, and since the logarithm is a one to one function, $k = 3$. Checking, $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = \log 3 - 0 = \log 3$, as required.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$, with $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = \log|x| + c$.
common_misconception: The student drops the logarithm on the right hand side and solves $\log k = 3$, producing $k = e^{3}$.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of a power function
concept_tested: Applying the power rule and both limits to a simple polynomial integrand
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} x^{3}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student substitutes the upper limit only and never subtracts the value at $x = 1$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student differentiates the integrand instead of integrating it, using $3x^{2}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student substitutes the difference of the limits into the antiderivative, computing $\dfrac{(2-1)^{4}}{4}$.

solution: An antiderivative of $x^{3}$ is $\dfrac{x^{4}}{4}$. By the fundamental theorem, $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} x^{3}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{4}}{4}\right]_{1}^{2} = \dfrac{2^{4}}{4} - \dfrac{1^{4}}{4} = \dfrac{16}{4} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{15}{4}$. Note that the substitution must be done separately at each limit and then subtracted; the difference of the limits is never substituted into the antiderivative.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} x^{n}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\right]_{a}^{b}$ for $n \ne -1$.
common_misconception: The student evaluates the antiderivative at the upper limit alone and forgets to subtract its value at the lower limit.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of a power function
concept_tested: Handling a fractional index in a definite integral
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} \sqrt{x}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student raises the index correctly but forgets to divide by $\dfrac{3}{2}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student multiplies by $\dfrac{3}{2}$ instead of dividing by it.
distractor_rationale.C: The student differentiates $\sqrt{x}$ rather than integrating it.

solution: Write $\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{4} x^{1/2}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{3/2}}{3/2}\right]_{0}^{4} = \left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{0}^{4}$. Now $4^{3/2} = \left(\sqrt{4}\right)^{3} = 2^{3} = 8$, so the value is $\dfrac{2}{3}(8) - \dfrac{2}{3}(0) = \dfrac{16}{3}$. The integrand is continuous on $[0, 4]$, since $\sqrt{x}$ is defined and continuous for $x \ge 0$, so the fundamental theorem applies.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int x^{n}\,dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + c$ for $n \ne -1$; here $n = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
common_misconception: The student raises the index by one but divides by the old index or by nothing at all.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of a power function
concept_tested: Integrating a negative power and keeping the sign of the antiderivative
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{1}{x^{3}}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student substitutes the lower limit first and subtracts in the wrong order.
distractor_rationale.B: The student integrates $x^{3}$ in place of $x^{-3}$, ignoring that the power is negative.
distractor_rationale.D: The student divides by $-4$ instead of $-2$, using the old index in the denominator.

solution: Write $\dfrac{1}{x^{3}} = x^{-3}$. Raising the index by one gives $x^{-2}$ and dividing by the new index $-2$ gives the antiderivative $-\dfrac{1}{2x^{2}}$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} x^{-3}\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{1}{2x^{2}}\right]_{1}^{2} = -\dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{8}$. The integrand has a pole at $x = 0$, but $0$ does not lie in $[1, 2]$, so the integrand is continuous there and the answer is valid. The value is positive, as it must be, since the integrand is positive on $[1, 2]$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int x^{-3}\,dx = \dfrac{x^{-2}}{-2} + c = -\dfrac{1}{2x^{2}} + c$.
common_misconception: The student loses track of the sign produced by the negative index and reports the negative of the correct value.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of a power function
concept_tested: Recovering an unknown upper limit from a given value of the integral
stem: If $a > 0$ and $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{a} 2x\,dx = 8$, then $a$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student substitutes the limits into the integrand itself and solves $2a - 2 = 8$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student drops the contribution of the lower limit and solves $a^{2} = 8$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student solves correctly for $a^{2}$ but reports that value as $a$.

solution: An antiderivative of $2x$ is $x^{2}$, so $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{a} 2x\,dx = \left[x^{2}\right]_{1}^{a} = a^{2} - 1$. Setting $a^{2} - 1 = 8$ gives $a^{2} = 9$, so $a = 3$ or $a = -3$. The condition $a > 0$ selects $a = 3$. Checking, $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3} 2x\,dx = 9 - 1 = 8$, as required. The lower limit must be carried through; dropping it would give $a^{2} = 8$ and a value that does not satisfy the equation.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$, with $\displaystyle\int 2x\,dx = x^{2} + c$.
common_misconception: The student forgets the term contributed by the lower limit and solves $a^{2} = 8$.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of a trigonometric function
concept_tested: Using the antiderivative of the sine and substituting the limits
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.B: The student treats $\sin x$ as its own antiderivative and computes $\sin \pi - \sin 0$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses $\cos x$ as the antiderivative and loses the minus sign.
distractor_rationale.D: The student computes $-\cos \pi$ and forgets to subtract the value at the lower limit.

solution: An antiderivative of $\sin x$ is $-\cos x$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x\,dx = \left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi} = -\cos \pi - \left(-\cos 0\right) = -(-1) + 1 = 2$. The value is positive, which is consistent with $\sin x \ge 0$ throughout $[0, \pi]$. The minus sign in the antiderivative must be kept; using $\cos x$ instead would give $-2$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + c$.
common_misconception: The student writes the antiderivative of $\sin x$ as $\cos x$, dropping the minus sign.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of a trigonometric function
concept_tested: Integrating a trigonometric function of a multiple angle
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/6} \cos 3x\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student writes the antiderivative as $\sin 3x$ and forgets to divide by $3$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student multiplies by $3$ instead of dividing by it.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by $3$ correctly but substitutes the limit into $\sin x$ rather than $\sin 3x$.

solution: An antiderivative of $\cos 3x$ is $\dfrac{\sin 3x}{3}$, since differentiating it returns $\dfrac{3\cos 3x}{3} = \cos 3x$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/6} \cos 3x\,dx = \left[\dfrac{\sin 3x}{3}\right]_{0}^{\pi/6} = \dfrac{1}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\sin 0 = \dfrac{1}{3}(1) - 0 = \dfrac{1}{3}$. Note that the angle at the upper limit is $3 \times \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, not $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int \cos(kx)\,dx = \dfrac{\sin(kx)}{k} + c$ for a constant $k \ne 0$.
common_misconception: The student omits the factor $\dfrac{1}{3}$ that comes from integrating a function of $3x$.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of a trigonometric function
concept_tested: Evaluating an integral whose antiderivative is a logarithm of a trigonometric function
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \tan x\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student takes $\sec \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ to be $2$ instead of $\sqrt{2}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses $\log|\cos x|$ as the antiderivative, omitting the minus sign.
distractor_rationale.D: The student uses $\log\left|\sec^{2}x\right|$ as the antiderivative and evaluates $\log 4$.

solution: An antiderivative of $\tan x$ is $\log|\sec x|$. Since $\cos x > 0$ on $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$, the modulus may be dropped there. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \tan x\,dx = \left[\log|\sec x|\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \log\left(\sec\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - \log\left(\sec 0\right) = \log\sqrt{2} - \log 1 = \log 2^{1/2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\log 2$. The step $\log\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\log 2$ uses the law $\log a^{m} = m\log a$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int \tan x\,dx = \log|\sec x| + c = -\log|\cos x| + c$.
common_misconception: The student misreads $\sec\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ as $2$, or drops the minus sign when using $\log|\cos x|$.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of a trigonometric function
concept_tested: Splitting the interval where the integrand changes sign inside a modulus
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} \left|\cos x\right|\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student ignores the modulus and integrates $\cos x$ over the whole interval.
distractor_rationale.B: The student handles the modulus correctly but stops at $x = \pi$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student doubles the answer once too often after using the symmetry of the graph.

solution: On $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and on $\left[\dfrac{3\pi}{2}, 2\pi\right]$ we have $\cos x \ge 0$, while on $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ we have $\cos x \le 0$. So the integral is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos x\,dx - \int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2}\cos x\,dx + \int_{3\pi/2}^{2\pi}\cos x\,dx$. These are $\left[\sin x\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} = 1$, then $-\left[\sin x\right]_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} = -(-1 - 1) = 2$, then $\left[\sin x\right]_{3\pi/2}^{2\pi} = 0 - (-1) = 1$. Adding, the value is $1 + 2 + 1 = 4$. Without the modulus the three signed pieces would cancel to $0$, so the modulus is what makes the answer non-zero.
formula_principle: If the integrand changes sign inside $[a, b]$, split the interval at those points and use $|f(x)| = f(x)$ where $f \ge 0$ and $|f(x)| = -f(x)$ where $f \le 0$.
common_misconception: The student integrates $\cos x$ straight through and reports $0$, forgetting that the modulus removes the cancellation.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of an exponential or logarithmic function
concept_tested: Using the logarithmic antiderivative of the reciprocal function
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e^{2}} \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student integrates $\dfrac{1}{x}$ as if the integrand were $e^{x}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student substitutes the upper limit into the integrand instead of the antiderivative.
distractor_rationale.C: The student writes $\log e^{2}$ as $1$, treating the index as part of the base.

solution: On $\left[1, e^{2}\right]$ the integrand $\dfrac{1}{x}$ is continuous and positive, so $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e^{2}} \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = \left[\log|x|\right]_{1}^{e^{2}} = \log e^{2} - \log 1 = 2 - 0 = 2$, using $\log e^{2} = 2\log e = 2$ and $\log 1 = 0$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = \log|x| + c$, and $\log e^{m} = m$.
common_misconception: The student forgets that $\log e^{2} = 2$ and leaves the answer in exponential form.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of an exponential or logarithmic function
concept_tested: Integrating an exponential function with a linear multiple in the index
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} e^{2x}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student forgets to divide by $2$ when integrating $e^{2x}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by $2$ but omits the value at the lower limit.
distractor_rationale.D: The student multiplies by $2$ instead of dividing by it.

solution: An antiderivative of $e^{2x}$ is $\dfrac{e^{2x}}{2}$, since differentiating it gives $\dfrac{2e^{2x}}{2} = e^{2x}$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} e^{2x}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{e^{2x}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{e^{0}}{2} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{e^{2} - 1}{2}$. The term $\dfrac{1}{2}$ from the lower limit must not be dropped, since $e^{0} = 1$ and not $0$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int e^{kx}\,dx = \dfrac{e^{kx}}{k} + c$ for a constant $k \ne 0$.
common_misconception: The student assumes $e^{0} = 0$ and drops the contribution of the lower limit.

subtopic: Direct evaluation of a definite integral of an exponential or logarithmic function
concept_tested: Evaluating a definite integral of the logarithmic function using integration by parts
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e} \log x\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student uses $x\log x$ as the antiderivative and omits the term $-x$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student integrates $e^{x}$ in place of $\log x$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student gets the antiderivative right but adds the value at the lower limit instead of subtracting it.

solution: Take $u = \log x$ and $dv = dx$, so $du = \dfrac{1}{x}dx$ and $v = x$. Then $\displaystyle\int \log x\,dx = x\log x - \int x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx = x\log x - x + c$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e} \log x\,dx = \left[x\log x - x\right]_{1}^{e} = \left(e\log e - e\right) - \left(1 \cdot \log 1 - 1\right) = (e - e) - (0 - 1) = 0 + 1 = 1$. The integrand is continuous on $[1, e]$ because $x > 0$ there.
formula_principle: By parts with $u = \log x$ and $dv = dx$, $\displaystyle\int \log x\,dx = x\log x - x + c$ for $x > 0$.
common_misconception: The student stops at $x\log x$ and never subtracts the second term $x$ of the antiderivative.

subtopic: Definite integrals of rational functions reducing to a logarithm or an inverse tangent
concept_tested: Recognising the standard inverse tangent form
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.B: The student uses $\sin^{-1}x$ as the antiderivative and evaluates $\sin^{-1}1$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student recalls the wrong principal value and takes $\tan^{-1}1$ as $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student treats $\dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}$ like $\dfrac{1}{1 + x}$ and produces a logarithm.

solution: An antiderivative of $\dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}$ is $\tan^{-1}x$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx = \left[\tan^{-1}x\right]_{0}^{1} = \tan^{-1}1 - \tan^{-1}0 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - 0 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, taking principal values. The denominator $1 + x^{2}$ never vanishes, so the integrand is continuous everywhere and the fundamental theorem applies.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx = \tan^{-1}x + c$, with $\tan^{-1}$ taking principal values in $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
common_misconception: The student confuses the inverse tangent form with the inverse sine form of the standard integral.

concept_tested: Evaluating a linear denominator that gives a difference of logarithms
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{x + 2}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student substitutes the upper limit only and never subtracts the value at $x = 0$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student substitutes the lower limit only and reports that value.
distractor_rationale.D: The student adds the two logarithms instead of subtracting them.

solution: An antiderivative of $\dfrac{1}{x + 2}$ is $\log|x + 2|$. On $[0, 1]$ we have $x + 2 > 0$, so the modulus may be dropped there and the integrand is continuous, the pole $x = -2$ being outside the interval. common_misconception: The student subtracts the logarithms incorrectly, or forgets the value at the lower limit entirely.

solution: Here $a^{2} = 4$, so $a = 2$ and the antiderivative is $\dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{2}$. subtopic: Definite integrals of rational functions reducing to a logarithm or an inverse tangent
concept_tested: Reducing an improper rational integrand before using the inverse tangent form
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x^{2}}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student writes $\dfrac{x^{2}}{1 + x^{2}}$ as $\dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}} - 1$, reversing the two terms.
distractor_rationale.B: The student cancels $x^{2}$ against the $x^{2}$ in the denominator and integrates $\dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student splits the integrand correctly but adds the inverse tangent term instead of subtracting it.

solution: Write $\dfrac{x^{2}}{1 + x^{2}} = \dfrac{\left(1 + x^{2}\right) - 1}{1 + x^{2}} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x^{2}}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx = \int_{0}^{1} 1\,dx - \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}\,dx = \left[x\right]_{0}^{1} - \left[\tan^{-1}x\right]_{0}^{1} = 1 - \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Since $\dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx 0.785$, the answer is about $0.215$, which is positive as it must be because the integrand is non-negative on $[0, 1]$.
formula_principle: When the degree of the numerator is not less than the degree of the denominator, divide first: $\dfrac{x^{2}}{1 + x^{2}} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{1 + x^{2}}$.
common_misconception: The student cancels $x^{2}$ between the numerator and the denominator instead of performing the division.

stem: To evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos x\,\sqrt{1 + \sin x}\,dx$ the substitution $t = 1 + \sin x$ is used. The new limits of integration for $t$ are

distractor_rationale.B: The student changes the variable but carries the original limits of $x$ across unchanged.

solution: With $t = 1 + \sin x$ we get $dt = \cos x\,dx$. subtopic: Substitution in a definite integral with the limits changed
concept_tested: Substituting a logarithm and converting the limits to logarithmic values
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{\log x}{x}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student integrates $t$ as $t^{2}$ and forgets to divide by $2$.

solution: Put $t = \log x$, so $dt = \dfrac{1}{x}\,dx$. The limits change: when $x = 1$, $t = \log 1 = 0$; when $x = 2$, $t = \log 2$. The new lower limit is $0$, not $1$, because $\log 1 = 0$; this is the step most often missed.
formula_principle: With $t = \log x$, $dt = \dfrac{1}{x}dx$, and the limits become $\log a$ and $\log b$.
common_misconception: The student converts the integrand to $t$ but keeps $1$ and $2$ as the limits instead of $0$ and $\log 2$.

subtopic: Substitution in a definite integral where a student forgets to change the limits
concept_tested: Changing the limits when a linear substitution is made
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} \left(2x - 1\right)^{3}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.B: The student substitutes $t = 2x - 1$, reaches $\dfrac{t^{4}}{8}$, and then evaluates it at $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, the original limits of $x$, instead of the new limits $t = 1$ and $t = 3$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student changes the limits correctly but forgets that $dx = \dfrac{dt}{2}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student both keeps the original limits and omits the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ from $dx$.

solution: Put $t = 2x - 1$, so $dt = 2\,dx$, that is $dx = \dfrac{dt}{2}$. The limits change with the variable: when $x = 1$, $t = 2(1) - 1 = 1$; when $x = 2$, $t = 2(2) - 1 = 3$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\left(2x - 1\right)^{3}dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{3} t^{3}\,dt = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{t^{4}}{4}\right]_{1}^{3} = \dfrac{1}{8}\left(81 - 1\right) = \dfrac{80}{8} = 10$. Equivalently, return to $x$ first: $\dfrac{\left(2x-1\right)^{4}}{8}$ evaluated from $x = 1$ to $x = 2$ gives $\dfrac{81 - 1}{8} = 10$. The two routes agree, but mixing them, by using the $t$ form with the $x$ limits, does not.
formula_principle: If $t = g(x)$, then $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f\left(g(x)\right)g'(x)\,dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(t)\,dt$. Once the variable is $t$, the limits must be values of $t$.
common_misconception: The student writes the antiderivative in $t$ and then substitutes the original $x$ limits into it, because the limits were never changed when the variable was.

subtopic: Substitution in a definite integral where a student forgets to change the limits
concept_tested: Knowing the two permitted ways of finishing a substitution in a definite integral
stem: A definite integral $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ is being evaluated by the substitution $t = g(x)$. Which of the following procedures is correct?

options.A: Keep the limits $a$ and $b$ throughout, since the limits belong to the integral and not to the variable.
options.B: Either replace the limits by $g(a)$ and $g(b)$ and finish in $t$, or return the antiderivative to the variable $x$ and then use $a$ and $b$.
options.C: Replace the limits by $g(a)$ and $g(b)$, and also return the antiderivative to the variable $x$ before substituting.
options.D: Keep the limits $a$ and $b$, and add the constant of integration before substituting them.

correct_answer_text: Either replace the limits by $g(a)$ and $g(b)$ and finish in $t$, or return the antiderivative to the variable $x$ and then use $a$ and $b$.

distractor_rationale.A: The student believes the limits are fixed labels of the integral rather than values of the variable of integration.
distractor_rationale.C: The student applies both corrections at once and changes the limits twice over.
distractor_rationale.D: The student thinks the arbitrary constant repairs the mismatch created by not changing the limits.

solution: The limits of a definite integral are values of whatever variable is being integrated. If the integral is rewritten in $t$, the limits must be the corresponding values of $t$, namely $g(a)$ and $g(b)$. Alternatively one may find the antiderivative in $t$, replace $t$ by $g(x)$ to return to the original variable, and only then substitute the original limits $a$ and $b$. Both routes give the same value. What must never be done is to use the $t$ form of the antiderivative together with the $x$ limits, since those two belong to different variables. Adding an arbitrary constant does not help, because a constant cancels in the subtraction and cannot repair a mismatch of limits.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f\left(g(x)\right)g'(x)\,dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(t)\,dt$; the limits are values of the variable of integration, so they change when the variable changes.
common_misconception: The student treats the limits as fixed properties of the integral sign and leaves them unchanged after a substitution.

subtopic: Substitution in a definite integral where a student forgets to change the limits
concept_tested: Detecting a limit mismatch when the substitution is the tangent function
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \tan x\,\sec^{2}x\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student reaches $\dfrac{t^{2}}{2}$ with $t = \tan x$ and then substitutes the original limits $0$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ for $t$, never having changed them to $0$ and $1$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student changes the limits correctly but integrates $t$ as $t^{2}$ without dividing by $2$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student both keeps the original limits and omits the division by $2$.

solution: Put $t = \tan x$, so $dt = \sec^{2}x\,dx$. The limits change: when $x = 0$, $t = \tan 0 = 0$; when $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $t = \tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\tan x\,\sec^{2}x\,dx = \int_{0}^{1} t\,dt = \left[\dfrac{t^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Returning instead to $x$ gives $\left[\dfrac{\tan^{2}x}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \dfrac{1}{2} - 0 = \dfrac{1}{2}$, the same value. The integrand is continuous on $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$, since $\sec x$ is finite there.
formula_principle: With $t = \tan x$, $dt = \sec^{2}x\,dx$, and the limits become $\tan a$ and $\tan b$.
common_misconception: The student keeps $0$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ as the limits after changing the variable to $t$, so an answer containing $\pi^{2}$ appears where a rational number is expected.

subtopic: Definite integrals requiring an algebraic or trigonometric simplification first
concept_tested: Reducing a squared trigonometric function by the double angle identity
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^{2}x\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student replaces $\sin^{2}x$ by $1 - \cos 2x$ and forgets to halve it.
distractor_rationale.C: The student integrates $\sin^{2}x$ as $\dfrac{\sin^{3}x}{3}$, applying the power rule to a function of $x$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student halves the expression a second time while integrating the constant term.

solution: The power $\sin^{2}x$ has no direct antiderivative, so reduce it first: $\sin^{2}x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{2}x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left(1 - \cos 2x\right)dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[x - \dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}$. At the upper limit this is $\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\sin \pi}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 0$, and at the lower limit it is $0$. Hence the value is $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
formula_principle: $\sin^{2}x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$, after which each term is a standard integral.
common_misconception: The student applies the power rule to $\sin^{2}x$ as though $\sin x$ were the variable of integration.

subtopic: Definite integrals requiring an algebraic or trigonometric simplification first
concept_tested: Splitting an algebraic fraction term by term before integrating
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{x^{2} + 1}{x}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student splits the fraction correctly but attaches the wrong sign to the logarithmic term.
distractor_rationale.B: The student integrates only the term $x$ and discards $\dfrac{1}{x}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student substitutes the upper limit only and never subtracts the value at $x = 1$.

solution: Splitting the fraction, $\dfrac{x^{2} + 1}{x} = x + \dfrac{1}{x}$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\left(x + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2} + \log|x|\right]_{1}^{2} = \left(\dfrac{4}{2} + \log 2\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \log 1\right) = \left(2 + \log 2\right) - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} + \log 2$. The interval $[1, 2]$ avoids the pole at $x = 0$, so the integrand is continuous. There is no rule for integrating a quotient directly, which is why the division must be done first.
formula_principle: Divide term by term first: $\dfrac{x^{2} + 1}{x} = x + \dfrac{1}{x}$, then integrate each piece.
common_misconception: The student tries to integrate the quotient as a whole instead of dividing the numerator term by term.

subtopic: Definite integrals requiring an algebraic or trigonometric simplification first
concept_tested: Using a double angle identity to turn a rational trigonometric integrand into a standard form
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{1}{1 + \cos 2x}\,dx$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student writes $1 + \cos 2x$ as $\cos^{2}x$ and loses the factor $2$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student halves the result a second time after integrating $\sec^{2}x$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student replaces $1 + \cos 2x$ by the constant $2$ and integrates $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

solution: The integrand looks like a rational function, but the identity $\cos 2x = 2\cos^{2}x - 1$ gives $1 + \cos 2x = 2\cos^{2}x$. Hence $\dfrac{1}{1 + \cos 2x} = \dfrac{1}{2\cos^{2}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sec^{2}x$. Therefore $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\dfrac{1}{1 + \cos 2x}\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\sec^{2}x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\tan x\right]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - 0\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$. On $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$ we have $\cos x \ne 0$, so the integrand is continuous and no pole lies inside the interval.
formula_principle: $1 + \cos 2x = 2\cos^{2}x$, so $\dfrac{1}{1 + \cos 2x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sec^{2}x$, and $\displaystyle\int \sec^{2}x\,dx = \tan x + c$.
common_misconception: The student attacks the integrand as a rational function instead of recognising $1 + \cos 2x = 2\cos^{2}x$.

subtopic: The constant of integration and why it does not appear in a definite integral
concept_tested: Explaining why the arbitrary constant is omitted in a definite integral
stem: While evaluating $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ by the fundamental theorem, the constant of integration is not written because

options.A: it occurs at both limits and cancels in the subtraction $\left(F(b) + c\right) - \left(F(a) + c\right)$.
options.B: a definite integral does not have an antiderivative, so no constant ever arises.
options.C: the constant of integration is always zero when the limits of integration are numbers.
options.D: the limits of integration are written in place of the constant of integration.

correct_answer_text: it occurs at both limits and cancels in the subtraction $\left(F(b) + c\right) - \left(F(a) + c\right)$.

distractor_rationale.B: The student thinks the antiderivative belongs only to the indefinite integral.
distractor_rationale.C: The student believes the arbitrary constant takes the particular value zero here.
distractor_rationale.D: The student treats the limits as a substitute for the constant rather than as values to be substituted.

solution: The fundamental theorem allows any antiderivative of $f$ to be used. Take the general antiderivative $F(x) + c$. Substituting the limits gives $\left(F(b) + c\right) - \left(F(a) + c\right) = F(b) - F(a) + c - c = F(b) - F(a)$. The constant appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so it cancels, and the value of the definite integral is the same whichever antiderivative is chosen. This is why the constant is simply omitted from the start. It is not that the constant is zero; it is that its value never affects the answer.
formula_principle: If $F' = f$, then every antiderivative of $f$ has the form $F(x) + c$, and $\left(F(b) + c\right) - \left(F(a) + c\right) = F(b) - F(a)$.
common_misconception: The student believes the arbitrary constant is set to zero in a definite integral, rather than seeing that it cancels.

subtopic: The constant of integration and why it does not appear in a definite integral
concept_tested: Comparing two antiderivatives that differ by an added constant
stem: To evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} 3x^{2}\,dx$, one student uses the antiderivative $F(x) = x^{3}$ and another uses $G(x) = x^{3} + 7$. Then

options.A: the first obtains $8$ and the second obtains $15$, because $G$ carries the extra term.
options.B: the first obtains $8$ and the second obtains $22$, because $G$ carries the extra term twice.
options.C: neither result is valid, because an antiderivative must be written with an arbitrary constant.
options.D: both obtain $8$, because the added $7$ cancels when the limits are substituted.

correct_answer_text: both obtain $8$, because the added $7$ cancels when the limits are substituted.

distractor_rationale.A: The student adds the constant once, at the upper limit only, instead of at both limits.
distractor_rationale.B: The student adds the constant at both limits with the same sign instead of subtracting.
distractor_rationale.C: The student insists on the arbitrary constant and does not see that it cancels on subtraction.

solution: With $F(x) = x^{3}$, the value is $F(2) - F(0) = 8 - 0 = 8$. With $G(x) = x^{3} + 7$, the value is $G(2) - G(0) = (8 + 7) - (0 + 7) = 15 - 7 = 8$. The $7$ is added at the upper limit and subtracted again at the lower limit, so it disappears. Both students are right, and both antiderivatives are legitimate since $G'(x) = 3x^{2} = F'(x)$. The error in the other readings is to add the constant only once, or to add it twice with the same sign.
formula_principle: Two antiderivatives of the same function on an interval differ by a constant, and that constant cancels in $F(b) - F(a)$.
common_misconception: The student substitutes the added constant at the upper limit but forgets that it also appears at the lower limit.

subtopic: The constant of integration and why it does not appear in a definite integral
concept_tested: Recognising that antiderivatives differing by a constant give the same definite integral
stem: For $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ on $[1, 4]$, one student uses the antiderivative $F(x) = \log|x|$ and another uses $G(x) = \log|5x|$. The values of $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{4} f(x)\,dx$ that they obtain are

options.A: $\log 4$ from the first and $\log 20$ from the second, since the two antiderivatives are different functions.
options.B: $\log 4$ from both, since $G(x) - F(x) = \log 5$ is a constant.
options.C: $\log 4$ from the first and $5\log 4$ from the second, since the factor $5$ multiplies the answer.
options.D: $\log 3$ from both, since only the difference of the limits matters.

correct_answer_text: $\log 4$ from both, since $G(x) - F(x) = \log 5$ is a constant.

distractor_rationale.A: The student substitutes the upper limit into $G$ and forgets that the lower limit also carries the factor $5$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student pulls the $5$ out as a multiplier of the whole integral instead of as an added logarithm.
distractor_rationale.D: The student substitutes the difference of the limits into the antiderivative instead of subtracting the two values.

solution: Both are genuine antiderivatives of $\dfrac{1}{x}$, since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\log|5x|\right] = \dfrac{5}{5x} = \dfrac{1}{x}$. With $F$, the value is $\log 4 - \log 1 = \log 4$. With $G$, the value is $\log 20 - \log 5 = \log\dfrac{20}{5} = \log 4$. The two agree because $\log|5x| = \log 5 + \log|x|$, so $G$ and $F$ differ by the constant $\log 5$, which cancels in the subtraction. The interval $[1, 4]$ avoids $x = 0$, so the integrand is continuous throughout.
formula_principle: If $G(x) - F(x)$ is constant on an interval, then $G(b) - G(a) = F(b) - F(a)$, so both give the same definite integral.
common_misconception: The student treats $\log|5x|$ as $5\log|x|$, or applies the extra $\log 5$ at the upper limit only.

subtopic: Reversing the limits changes the sign
concept_tested: Reading off the value of an integral when the two limits are exchanged
stem: For a function $f$ continuous on $[2, 5]$ it is given that $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx = 7$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{5}^{2} f(x)\,dx$ is

distractor_rationale.B: The student believes the value of a definite integral does not depend on the order of the limits.
distractor_rationale.C: The student thinks exchanging the limits inverts the value, by false analogy with a ratio.
distractor_rationale.D: The student adds the two integrals in his head, gets zero, and reports that as the answer to the second one.

solution: Let $F$ be an antiderivative of $f$. By the fundamental theorem, $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx = F(5) - F(2) = 7$. For the reversed integral, $\displaystyle\int_{5}^{2} f(x)\,dx = F(2) - F(5)$, which is the negative of the previous difference. Hence its value is $-7$. Note that the two integrals add to zero, which is exactly the statement $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f + \int_{5}^{2} f = \int_{2}^{2} f = 0$, but each one separately is $\pm 7$.
formula_principle: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ then $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = -\int_{b}^{a} f(x)\,dx$.
common_misconception: The student treats a definite integral as if it were unaffected by the order in which the limits are written.

subtopic: Reversing the limits changes the sign
concept_tested: Evaluating an integral written with the larger number as the lower limit
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{3}^{1} x^{2}\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.B: The student silently rewrites the integral with the smaller number as the lower limit.
distractor_rationale.C: The student writes $\dfrac{1^{3} + 3^{3}}{3}$ instead of $\dfrac{1^{3} - 3^{3}}{3}$ while keeping the leading sign.
distractor_rationale.D: The student both adds the cubes and reorders the limits.

solution: An antiderivative of $x^{2}$ is $\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}$. Substituting the upper limit first, $\displaystyle\int_{3}^{1} x^{2}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{3}^{1} = \dfrac{1^{3}}{3} - \dfrac{3^{3}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} - 9 = -\dfrac{26}{3}$. The same value follows from the reversal property, since $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{3} x^{2}\,dx = 9 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{26}{3}$ and reversing the limits changes only the sign.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} x^{n}\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\right]_{a}^{b}$, the upper limit being substituted first.
common_misconception: The student substitutes the numerically smaller limit first out of habit and loses the minus sign.

subtopic: Reversing the limits changes the sign
concept_tested: Recovering a limit of integration from a negative value of the integral
stem: If $a > 0$ and $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{1} 2x\,dx = -3$, then $a =$

distractor_rationale.A: The student solves $a^{2} = 4$ correctly but ignores the condition $a > 0$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student stops at $a^{2} = 4$ and reports that as the value of $a$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student turns $1 - a^{2} = -3$ into $a^{2} = 3 - 1$ by moving the terms with the wrong signs.

solution: An antiderivative of $2x$ is $x^{2}$, so $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{1} 2x\,dx = 1^{2} - a^{2} = 1 - a^{2}$. Setting this equal to $-3$ gives $1 - a^{2} = -3$, that is $a^{2} = 4$, so $a = 2$ or $a = -2$. The condition $a > 0$ leaves $a = 2$. The answer is consistent with the reversal property, since $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} 2x\,dx = 4 - 1 = 3$ and reversing the limits gives $-3$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$, so a negative value with a positive integrand means the lower limit exceeds the upper limit.
common_misconception: The student solves the resulting quadratic but forgets that the stem restricts the sign of the unknown limit.

subtopic: Splitting the interval at an interior point
concept_tested: Using additivity of the interval to find the missing piece
stem: For a continuous function $f$ it is given that $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\,dx = 5$ and $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{5} f(x)\,dx = 12$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student adds the two given values instead of subtracting.
distractor_rationale.B: The student multiplies the two given values, treating the integral as multiplicative over the interval.
distractor_rationale.C: The student subtracts in the wrong order and reports $5 - 12$.

solution: Split the interval $[0, 5]$ at the interior point $x = 2$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{5} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{2} f(x)\,dx + \int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx$. Substituting the given values, $12 = 5 + \displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx$, so $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx = 12 - 5 = 7$. The splitting property holds for any interior point and does not require $f$ to be positive.
formula_principle: For $a < c < b$, $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{c} f(x)\,dx + \int_{c}^{b} f(x)\,dx$.
common_misconception: The student adds the two given integrals instead of removing the part already counted.

subtopic: Splitting the interval at an interior point
concept_tested: Splitting at the point where the modulus changes its definition
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3} \left|x\right|\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.B: The student replaces $|x|$ by $x$ over the whole interval.
distractor_rationale.C: The student replaces $|x|$ by $-x$ over the whole interval.
distractor_rationale.D: The student doubles the integral from $0$ to $3$, treating the interval as if it were symmetric.

solution: The definition of $|x|$ changes at $x = 0$, which lies inside $[-2, 3]$, so split there. On $[-2, 0]$ we have $|x| = -x$, giving $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{0} (-x)\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{-2}^{0} = 0 - \left(-2\right) = 2$. On $[0, 3]$ we have $|x| = x$, giving $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3} x\,dx = \dfrac{9}{2}$. Adding the two pieces, $\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3} |x|\,dx = 2 + \dfrac{9}{2} = \dfrac{13}{2}$. The interval is not symmetric about $0$, so the even function shortcut does not apply here.
formula_principle: $|x| = -x$ for $x < 0$ and $|x| = x$ for $x \ge 0$, so the interval must be split at $x = 0$ before integrating.
common_misconception: The student integrates the modulus in one stroke without splitting at the point where its definition changes.

subtopic: Splitting the interval at an interior point
concept_tested: Integrating a function given by two different formulas on two subintervals
stem: A function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = 3x^{2}$ for $0 \le x \le 1$ and $f(x) = 2x + 1$ for $1 < x \le 2$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\,dx$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student uses the first formula on the whole interval $[0, 2]$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses the second formula on the whole interval $[0, 2]$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student splits the interval but integrates the second piece from $0$ to $2$ instead of from $1$ to $2$.

solution: The definition of $f$ changes at $x = 1$, so split there. On $[0, 1]$, $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} 3x^{2}\,dx = \left[x^{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = 1$. On $[1, 2]$, $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} (2x + 1)\,dx = \left[x^{2} + x\right]_{1}^{2} = (4 + 2) - (1 + 1) = 4$. Adding, $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} f(x)\,dx = 1 + 4 = 5$. The single point $x = 1$ where the two formulas meet does not affect the value of the integral.
formula_principle: For a function defined piecewise, split the interval at the point where the definition changes and use $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} f = \int_{0}^{1} f + \int_{1}^{2} f$.
common_misconception: The student picks one of the two formulas and integrates it over the entire interval.

subtopic: The property that the integral from 0 to a of f(x) equals the integral from 0 to a of f(a minus x)
concept_tested: Stating the reflection property on the interval from 0 to a
stem: For a continuous function $f$ on $[0, a]$, $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx$ is equal to

distractor_rationale.B: The student reflects with a plus sign, which moves the interval to $[a, 2a]$ instead of reversing it.
distractor_rationale.C: The student writes the reflection the wrong way round, obtaining the argument $x - a$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student keeps the minus sign produced by $dt = -dx$ after having already reversed the limits.

solution: Put $t = a - x$, so that $x = a - t$ and $dx = -dt$. When $x = 0$ we get $t = a$, and when $x = a$ we get $t = 0$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{0} f(a - t)(-dt) = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - t)\,dt$, where the minus sign has been used to exchange the limits. Since the variable of integration is a dummy, this is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\,dx$. The minus sign is consumed by the reversal of limits, so no minus sign survives in the final statement.
formula_principle: Putting $t = a - x$ gives $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\,dx$.
common_misconception: The student applies the substitution but keeps the minus sign as well as reversing the limits, so the sign is changed twice.

subtopic: The property that the integral from 0 to a of f(x) equals the integral from 0 to a of f(a minus x)
concept_tested: Using the reflection property to avoid expanding a high power
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} x\left(1 - x\right)^{5}\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.A: The student applies the property but integrates $x^{4} - x^{5}$, dropping one from each exponent.
distractor_rationale.B: The student keeps only the first term $\int_{0}^{1} x^{5}\,dx$ after applying the property.
distractor_rationale.D: The student integrates $x^{6} - x^{7}$, raising each exponent by one too many.

solution: Here $a = 1$, so replacing $x$ by $1 - x$ gives $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} x(1 - x)^{5}\,dx = \int_{0}^{1} (1 - x)\left[1 - (1 - x)\right]^{5}dx = \int_{0}^{1} (1 - x)x^{5}\,dx$. This is now a polynomial, $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\left(x^{5} - x^{6}\right)dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{6}}{6} - \dfrac{x^{7}}{7}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{6} - \dfrac{1}{7} = \dfrac{7 - 6}{42} = \dfrac{1}{42}$. The property has replaced the expansion of $(1 - x)^{5}$ by a two term integral.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\,dx$, used here with $a = 1$.
common_misconception: The student shifts the exponents by one while integrating the simplified polynomial.

subtopic: The property that the integral from 0 to a of f(x) equals the integral from 0 to a of f(a minus x)
concept_tested: Removing the factor x from an integrand by reflection
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} x\sin x\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.A: The student reaches $2I = 2\pi$ and reports the left side value without halving.
distractor_rationale.C: The student halves the correct answer once more.
distractor_rationale.D: The student calls $x\sin x$ an odd function and concludes that the integral vanishes.

solution: Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} x\sin x\,dx$. Replacing $x$ by $\pi - x$ gives $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}(\pi - x)\sin(\pi - x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{\pi}(\pi - x)\sin x\,dx$. Adding the two expressions for $I$, the terms in $x\sin x$ cancel and $2I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\pi\sin x\,dx = \pi\left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi} = \pi(1 + 1) = 2\pi$. Hence $I = \pi$. Integration by parts gives the same value, since $\left[-x\cos x + \sin x\right]_{0}^{\pi} = \pi$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\,dx$ with $a = \pi$, together with $\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x$.
common_misconception: The student stops at the equation for $2I$ and reports that number as the value of the integral.

subtopic: The property that the integral from a to b of f(x) equals the integral from a to b of f(a plus b minus x)
concept_tested: Forming the correct reflected argument on a general interval
stem: For a continuous function $f$ on $[2, 5]$, $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx$ is equal to

distractor_rationale.A: The student uses the difference of the limits instead of their sum.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses only the upper limit, as in the property for the interval starting at zero.
distractor_rationale.D: The student subtracts in the wrong order and writes $x - (a + b)$.

solution: Put $t = a + b - x$ with $a = 2$ and $b = 5$, so $t = 7 - x$ and $dx = -dt$. When $x = 2$ we get $t = 5$, and when $x = 5$ we get $t = 2$. Hence $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{5} f(x)\,dx = \int_{5}^{2} f(7 - t)(-dt) = \int_{2}^{5} f(7 - t)\,dt = \int_{2}^{5} f(7 - x)\,dx$. The reflection must send $2$ to $5$ and $5$ to $2$, and only $7 - x$ does that.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(a + b - x)\,dx$.
common_misconception: The student reflects about the wrong number, using $b - a$ or $b$ alone instead of $a + b$.

subtopic: The property that the integral from a to b of f(x) equals the integral from a to b of f(a plus b minus x)
concept_tested: Pairing an integrand with its reflection when the two add to one
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{\log x}{\log x + \log(3 - x)}\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.A: The student obtains $2I = 1$ and reports the total instead of $I$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student takes $2I$ to be $a + b = 3$ rather than $b - a = 1$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student expects the reflected integrand to be the negative of the original and concludes that the integral vanishes.

solution: Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{\log x}{\log x + \log(3 - x)}\,dx$. Since $a + b = 1 + 2 = 3$, replacing $x$ by $3 - x$ gives $I = \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{\log(3 - x)}{\log(3 - x) + \log x}\,dx$, because $3 - (3 - x) = x$. Adding the two forms, the numerators add to the common denominator, so $2I = \displaystyle\int_{1}^{2} 1\,dx = 2 - 1 = 1$, giving $I = \dfrac{1}{2}$. No antiderivative of the integrand is needed, and none is available in elementary form.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(a + b - x)\,dx$, here with $a + b = 3$.
common_misconception: The student stops at $2I$ and does not divide by two, or reflects about $b - a$ instead of $a + b$.

stem: $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{4} \dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{5 - x}}\,dx =$

subtopic: Using the a minus x property to evaluate an integral that has no elementary antiderivative
concept_tested: Pairing an integrand with its reflection when the two add to one
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x + \cos x}\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.B: The student obtains $2I = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and reports that value as $I$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by two twice, once for the pairing and once again out of habit.
distractor_rationale.D: The student expects the reflected integrand to be $-f(x)$ and concludes that the two halves cancel.

solution: Let $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x + \cos x}\,dx$. Replacing $x$ by $\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x$ interchanges $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, so $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x + \sin x}\,dx$. Adding the two forms, the numerators add to the denominator and $2I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} 1\,dx = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. Hence $I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$. The integrand has no elementary antiderivative, so this pairing is the only route available at this level.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x)\,dx$ with $a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cos x$ and $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \sin x$.

concept_tested: Combining the reflection property with a doubling of the angle
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log\left(\sin x\right)\,dx =$

Adding, $2I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin x\cos x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log\left(\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\log(\sin 2x)\,dx - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\log 2$. In the remaining integral put $t = 2x$, so $dx = \dfrac{dt}{2}$ and the limits $x = 0$, $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ become $t = 0$, $t = \pi$. This gives $\dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\log(\sin t)\,dt$. Since $\log\left(\sin(\pi - t)\right) = \log(\sin t)$, the property for the interval $[0, 2a]$ with $a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ gives $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\log(\sin t)\,dt = 2I$, so the remaining integral is $I$. Therefore $2I = I - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\log 2$, which gives $I = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\log 2$.

concept_tested: Stating the condition under which the integral from 0 to 2a doubles
stem: Let $f$ be continuous on $[0, 2a]$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx$ holds when

distractor_rationale.A: This is the condition under which the integral is zero, not double.
distractor_rationale.B: The student reflects about $a$ instead of about $2a$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student quotes a condition of periodicity, which is a different property.

solution: Split at the midpoint, $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx + \int_{a}^{2a} f(x)\,dx$. In the second piece put $t = 2a - x$, so $dx = -dt$, and the limits $x = a$, $x = 2a$ become $t = a$, $t = 0$. This gives $\displaystyle\int_{a}^{2a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(2a - t)\,dt$. Hence the whole integral is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a}\left[f(x) + f(2a - x)\right]dx$. If $f(2a - x) = f(x)$ the bracket is $2f(x)$ and the integral is $2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx$; if $f(2a - x) = -f(x)$ the bracket is zero and the integral vanishes.

common_misconception: The student remembers that the property has two cases but attaches the doubling to the wrong one.

concept_tested: Integrating the modulus of the sine over two of its periods
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} \left|\sin x\right|\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.A: The student drops the modulus and integrates $\sin x$ over a full period.
distractor_rationale.C: The student integrates over one period of $|\sin x|$ and forgets the second.
distractor_rationale.D: The student takes the period of $|\sin x|$ to be $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and counts four periods.

solution: The function $|\sin x|$ satisfies $|\sin(x + \pi)| = |-\sin x| = |\sin x|$, so its period is $\pi$, not $2\pi$. The interval $[0, 2\pi]$ therefore contains exactly two periods, and $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}|\sin x|\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{\pi}|\sin x|\,dx$. On $[0, \pi]$ the sine is non negative, so $|\sin x| = \sin x$ and $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx = \left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi} = 2$. Hence the value is $2\cdot 2 = 4$. Dropping the modulus would give $0$, because the two arches would then cancel.
formula_principle: $|\sin x|$ has period $\pi$, and $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{nT} f(x)\,dx = n\int_{0}^{T} f(x)\,dx$ for a function of period $T$.
common_misconception: The student integrates the sine itself over a full period and reports zero, ignoring the modulus.

stem: $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\left(x^{3}\cos x + \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\right)dx =$

Doubling gives $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and adding the zero from the odd term leaves $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

concept_tested: Integration by parts twice with a quadratic algebraic factor
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} x^{2}\sin x\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.A: The student substitutes only the upper limit, taking the whole antiderivative to be zero at $x = 0$.

solution: First application: $\int x^{2}\sin x\,dx = -x^{2}\cos x + 2\int x\cos x\,dx$. Second application: $\int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x$. common_misconception: Students stop after one application of the rule or lose the constant term $2\cos x$ at the lower limit.

solution: Let $I = \int e^{x}\sin x\,dx$. By parts twice, $I = e^{x}\sin x - \int e^{x}\cos x\,dx = e^{x}\sin x - e^{x}\cos x - I$, so $2I = e^{x}(\sin x - \cos x)$ and $I = \dfrac{e^{x}(\sin x - \cos x)}{2}$. Hence the integral is $\dfrac{e^{\pi/2}}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{e^{\pi/2} + 1}{2}$.

subtopic: Definite integrals of a modulus function, splitting at the point where the expression changes sign
concept_tested: Splitting the modulus of x at the origin over an interval that is not symmetric
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2} |x|\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.A: The student drops the modulus and integrates $x$ straight through, getting $\left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{-1}^{2}$, which is the classic wrong answer here.
distractor_rationale.C: The student integrates only over $[0, 2]$, believing the part to the left of the origin contributes nothing.
distractor_rationale.D: The student says $|x|$ is an even function and writes $2\int_{0}^{2}|x|\,dx$, applying the symmetry rule to an interval that is not symmetric about the origin.

solution: The expression inside the modulus changes sign at $x = 0$, which lies inside $[-1, 2]$. So $\int_{-1}^{2}|x|\,dx = \int_{-1}^{0}(-x)\,dx + \int_{0}^{2}x\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{-1}^{0} + \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{2} = \left(0 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 2 = \dfrac{5}{2}$.
formula_principle: $|x| = -x$ for $x < 0$ and $|x| = x$ for $x \ge 0$, with $\int_{a}^{b} = \int_{a}^{c} + \int_{c}^{b}$ splitting at the point where the sign changes.
common_misconception: Students integrate $x$ instead of $|x|$ over the whole interval and get $\dfrac{3}{2}$, never splitting at $x = 0$.

subtopic: Definite integrals of a modulus function, splitting at the point where the expression changes sign
concept_tested: Splitting the modulus of a linear expression at its zero
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2} |x - 1|\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.B: The student removes the modulus and integrates $x - 1$ over the whole interval, which is the standard wrong answer and cannot be right since the integrand is never negative.
distractor_rationale.C: The student integrates $x - 1$ without splitting and then takes the modulus of the final number instead of of the integrand.
distractor_rationale.D: The student integrates only over $[1, 2]$, where $x - 1 \ge 0$, and ignores the piece to the left of $x = 1$.

solution: The expression $x - 1$ changes sign at $x = 1$, which lies inside $[-1, 2]$. So $\int_{-1}^{2}|x-1|\,dx = \int_{-1}^{1}(1 - x)\,dx + \int_{1}^{2}(x - 1)\,dx$. Now $\int_{-1}^{1}(1-x)\,dx = \left[x - \dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{-1}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{2} - \left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) = 2$ and $\int_{1}^{2}(x-1)\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2} - x\right]_{1}^{2} = 0 - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$. The total is $\dfrac{5}{2}$.
formula_principle: $|x - 1| = 1 - x$ for $x < 1$ and $|x - 1| = x - 1$ for $x \ge 1$; split the interval at $x = 1$.
common_misconception: Students integrate $x - 1$ without the modulus and report $-\dfrac{3}{2}$, an impossible value for the integral of a function that is never negative.

solution: Since $a > 1$, the point $x = 1$ lies inside $[0, a]$. Now $\int_{0}^{1}(1 - x)\,dx = \left[x - \dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\int_{1}^{a}(x - 1)\,dx = \left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2} - x\right]_{1}^{a} = \dfrac{(a - 1)^{2}}{2}$. common_misconception: Students check only whether the integrand is negative somewhere, instead of locating the zeros of the integrand inside the interval.

concept_tested: Partial fractions with a linear numerator, and the shortcut hidden in it
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{2x + 3}{(x + 1)(x + 2)}\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.A: The student substitutes only the upper limit into $\log|(x+1)(x+2)|$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student takes the decomposition as $\dfrac{1}{x+1} - \dfrac{1}{x+2}$, giving the wrong sign to the second numerator.
distractor_rationale.D: The student evaluates the lower limit as $\log 1 + \log 3$, substituting $x = 1$ into the second factor by mistake.

solution: Write $\dfrac{2x+3}{(x+1)(x+2)} = \dfrac{A}{x+1} + \dfrac{B}{x+2}$. Then $A(x+2) + B(x+1) = 2x + 3$. Putting $x = -1$ gives $A = 1$ and putting $x = -2$ gives $B = 1$. So the integral is $\left[\log|x+1| + \log|x+2|\right]_{0}^{1} = (\log 2 + \log 3) - (\log 1 + \log 2) = \log 3$. The same answer follows in one step by noticing that the numerator is exactly $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{2} + 3x + 2\right)$, so the integral is $\left[\log|x^{2}+3x+2|\right]_{0}^{1} = \log 6 - \log 2 = \log 3$.
formula_principle: $\dfrac{2x+3}{(x+1)(x+2)} = \dfrac{1}{x+1} + \dfrac{1}{x+2}$; equivalently the numerator is the derivative of $x^{2} + 3x + 2$, so $\int\dfrac{2x+3}{x^{2}+3x+2}\,dx = \log|x^{2}+3x+2| + c$.
common_misconception: Students force a minus sign into every partial fraction decomposition, without solving for the two numerators.

concept_tested: Substituting x = a sin(theta) and changing the limits
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}\,dx =$

solution: Put $x = 2\sin\theta$, so $dx = 2\cos\theta\,d\theta$. When $x = 0$, $\theta = 0$, and when $x = 2$, $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$; these are the new limits. common_misconception: Students forget to change the limits to values of $\theta$ and substitute $x$ limits into a function of $\theta$.

concept_tested: Choosing the substitution that produces the stated new limits
stem: Which substitution turns $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{3}\sqrt{9 - x^{2}}\,dx$ into an integral in $\theta$ with lower limit $0$ and upper limit $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$?

subtopic: Comparing two definite integrals without evaluating either
concept_tested: Comparing two powers of x on the interval from 0 to 1
stem: Let $I_{1} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x^{2}\,dx$ and $I_{2} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}x^{3}\,dx$. Without evaluating either integral, which of the following is true?

distractor_rationale.A: The student assumes a higher power always gives a larger integral, forgetting that $0 \le x \le 1$ makes $x^{3} \le x^{2}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student assumes that integrals of powers of $x$ over the same interval must agree.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by the exponent instead of by the exponent increased by one, obtaining $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\dfrac{1}{4}$.

solution: For $0 < x < 1$ we have $x^{3} = x\cdot x^{2} < x^{2}$, since multiplying a positive number by $x < 1$ makes it smaller. The two integrands agree only at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$. Hence the integral of $x^{3}$ over $[0, 1]$ is strictly less than the integral of $x^{2}$ over the same interval, that is $I_{1} > I_{2}$. No evaluation is needed.
formula_principle: If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x$ in $[a, b]$, and the two are not identical, then $\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx < \int_{a}^{b}g(x)\,dx$.
common_misconception: Students carry over the idea that a bigger exponent means a bigger value, which is true for $x > 1$ but false on $[0, 1]$.

subtopic: Comparing two definite integrals without evaluating either
concept_tested: The comparison of two integrands depends on the interval chosen
stem: Which one of the following statements is true?

distractor_rationale.B: The student carries the comparison valid on $[0, 1]$ over to $[1, 2]$, where $x^{3} \ge x^{2}$ instead.
distractor_rationale.C: The student assumes a higher power always gives a larger integral.
distractor_rationale.D: The student notices the comparison on $[0, 1]$ and extends it to $[0, 2]$, where the part beyond $x = 1$ reverses the balance.

solution: On $(0, 1)$ we have $x^{3} < x^{2}$, so the first statement is true. On $(1, 2)$ the inequality reverses, since $x > 1$ gives $x^{3} > x^{2}$, so the second statement is false. The third contradicts the comparison on $(0,1)$. For the fourth, the interval $[0, 2]$ contains both behaviours, and the part beyond $x = 1$ dominates, so it fails as well. Only the first statement holds.
formula_principle: $f(x) \le g(x)$ on $[a, b]$ implies $\int_{a}^{b}f \le \int_{a}^{b}g$; the inequality between the integrands has to be checked on the interval actually used.
common_misconception: Students remember $x^{3} < x^{2}$ as a fact about the functions rather than as a fact that holds only for $0 < x < 1$.

concept_tested: Bounding an integral that cannot be evaluated by school methods
stem: For $I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\dfrac{dx}{1 + x^{4}}$, which of the following is true?

distractor_rationale.A: The student ignores that the integrand never exceeds $1$ on an interval of length $1$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses only the upper bound $1 + x^{4} \le 2$ and reads the resulting inequality the wrong way round.
distractor_rationale.D: The student replaces the integrand by its value at the midpoint of the interval and treats that as exact.

solution: For $0 \le x \le 1$ we have $0 \le x^{4} \le 1$, so $1 \le 1 + x^{4} \le 2$ and therefore $\dfrac{1}{2} \le \dfrac{1}{1+x^{4}} \le 1$. The length of the interval is $1 - 0 = 1$, so $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1 \le I \le 1\cdot 1$. Since the integrand equals $\dfrac{1}{2}$ only at $x = 1$ and equals $1$ only at $x = 0$, both inequalities are strict, giving $\dfrac{1}{2} < I < 1$.
formula_principle: If $m \le f(x) \le M$ on $[a, b]$ then $m(b - a) \le \int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx \le M(b - a)$, the two bounds being strict when $f$ is not constant.
common_misconception: Students try to find an antiderivative and give up, instead of bounding the integrand above and below on the interval.

subtopic: Definite integrals whose value is zero, and why
concept_tested: A product of an even and an odd factor is odd, so the integral vanishes
stem: $\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} x^{2}\sin x\,dx =$

distractor_rationale.A: The student calls the integrand even and computes $2\int_{0}^{\pi/2}x^{2}\sin x\,dx$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student integrates only over $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student integrates only over $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right]$.

solution: Let $f(x) = x^{2}\sin x$. Then $f(-x) = (-x)^{2}\sin(-x) = -x^{2}\sin x = -f(x)$, so $f$ is odd. The limits $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ are symmetric about the origin, so the integral is $0$. Doing the work by parts twice would give $\pi - 2$ for the right half and $2 - \pi$ for the left half, and these cancel.
formula_principle: An even function times an odd function is odd, and $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx = 0$ for an odd $f$.
common_misconception: Students see the even factor $x^{2}$ first and classify the whole integrand as even.

subtopic: Definite integrals whose value is zero, and why
concept_tested: Identifying which integral over a symmetric interval must vanish
stem: For every $a > 0$, which of the following definite integrals is equal to zero?

distractor_rationale.A: The student calls this odd because of the factor $x$, but odd times odd is even, so the integral is $2\int_{0}^{a}x\sin x\,dx$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student forgets that $\cos x$ is even, so this integral equals $2\sin a$, which is not always zero.
distractor_rationale.C: The student treats every integral over a symmetric interval as zero, although $x^{2}$ is even and positive.

solution: For $f(x) = x\cos x$: $f(-x) = (-x)\cos(-x) = -x\cos x = -f(x)$, so $f$ is odd and the integral over $[-a, a]$ is zero for every $a > 0$. In contrast $x\sin x$ is even, being odd times odd, and $\cos x$ and $x^{2}$ are even, so none of those three vanishes for all $a$.
formula_principle: $\displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx = 0$ when $f$ is odd; a product is odd only when one factor is odd and the other even.
common_misconception: Students judge oddness from the visible factor $x$ alone instead of testing $f(-x)$ for the whole integrand.

subtopic: Reverse reasoning: given the value of a definite integral, find a constant in the integrand
concept_tested: Finding an additive constant in a linear integrand from the value of the integral
stem: If $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} (2x + a)\,dx = 10$, then $a = $

distractor_rationale.A: The student takes $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} a\,dx$ as $a$ instead of $2a$ and solves $4 + a = 10$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student drops the term $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} 2x\,dx = 4$ and solves $2a = 10$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student uses $\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}$ as the antiderivative of $2x$, gets $2$ instead of $4$, and solves $2 + 2a = 10$.
